newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alcatel cuts first half loss, sees 1996 profit.
newsitem.headline: Alcatel cuts first half loss, sees 1996 profit.

text.p: France's largest industrial group Alcatel Alsthom, which posted the biggest loss in French corporate history for 1995, said Thursday it narrowed its losses in the first half and predicted a profit for 1996.

Chairman Serge Tchuruk said Alcatel is on line to break even for 1996, before asset gains, and that the sale of a 25 percent stake in mobile telecommunications company Cofira to British Telecommunications Plc would result in a 1996 profit of "several billion francs."

Cofira is a holding company controlled by Generale des Eaux. BT is buying the stake as part of a deal in which it takes a 25 percent participation in Generale's Cegetel, for 1.1 billion pounds ($1.7 billion) and the share capital of BT France.

Cofira, together with Vodafone and SBC Corp., owns France's second-biggest mobile telecoms group SFR. It will be included in Cegetel, a new Generale unit aiming to become France's second biggest telecommunications operator after France Telecom following liberalisation of the sector after 1998.

Alcatel said its first-half loss shrank to 400 million francs ($77.7 million) from 1.2 billion francs ($233.2 million) in the first six months of 1995. The 1996 loss was at the low end of analysts' expectations.
Operating income, however, fell to 500 million francs ($97.2 million) from 1.4 billion ($272.1 million). Sales edged down to 74.3 billion francs ($14.4 million) from 78.3 billion ($15.2 million).
Alcatel lost 26.6 billion ($5.2 billion) in 1995 after heavy charges.

"The board of directors noted that the results were in line with the action programme (announced last year) and reflected the recent trends and the still limited effects of the current recovery plan," Alcatel said in a statement.
The group reiterated its objective to achieve annual savings of 7 billion francs ($1.4 billion) by 1998.

Alcatel's telecoms segment widened its operating loss to 1.1 billion francs ($213.8 million) from 500 million ($97.2 million) but the group said the first half of 1996 was better than the prior half and it expected the division to post a profit in the 1996 second half.
Tchuruk said the unit's world market share in digital mobile telecoms was on course to reach 13 percent in 1997 and 15 percent in 1998 and its aim of 20 percent was achievable.
Tchuruk said that as part of the restructuring, Alcatel had announced 20,000 job losses since 1995. The group had 191,000 employees worldwide at the end of 1995.
